caveats: Covers lectures 1-7 of the 2026 edition only: 7 of the catalog's 90 recordings.

The decks of lectures 1-6 are flattened PDFs with no text layer and no printed slide numbers; slide N is PDF page N, and everything in their raw/slides/ files was read visually from 1280x720 page images, with no higher-resolution source. Lecture 7's deck is a Google Slides export with vector pages, a text layer and printed slide numbers equal to the pages; it was read from 1280x720 renders, with the text layer used for the spelling of printed prose.
Transcripts are YouTube auto-captions, lightly copy-edited. The verbatim captions are in raw/transcripts/original/.
Slide images are 1280x720, the native resolution of decks 1-6, below the 1400px used in sibling KBs; lecture 7's are 1400x788 renders.

Some slide code and formulas are reproduced as printed, including the slides' own slips (lecture 1: slide 82's tf.keras.optimizer, slide 86's update step; lecture 2: slide 27 writes matrix products with *, slide 28's 'from tf.keras.layers import SimpleRNN'; lecture 3: slides 53-54 pass filter_size where slide 47 uses kernel_size, slide 54 calls nn.Sequential with only torch imported, slide 65's loss has an unclosed parenthesis; lecture 4: slide 29's KL-divergence expansion carries a leading minus sign that makes it never positive, slide 41 overprints two labels and leaves an empty box where beta would go; lecture 5: slide 42 labels its third point (s_2, a_3, r_2); lecture 6: slide 41's callout names the weights theta while its formula writes W, and slides 60 and 61 label the same final image 'T0 (end)' and 'T-5 (end)'; lecture 7: slide 16's timeline labels GPT-3 '(2020)' but dates it 2022, and slide 28's quotation ends with an unmatched closing quote); the slide files note each one.
Lecture 2's slides and lecturer call the scaled dot product of query and key the 'cosine similarity', and give its denominator only as 'scaling'; the wiki reports this as the course states it.
Lecture 2 says vision transformers will be covered in lecture 3; lecture 3 as delivered covers convolutional networks and does not mention them.

Lecture 4's GAN objective (slides 70-72) is printed as log D(G(z)) + log(1 - D(x)) with the first term labelled 'Fake'; the lecturer reads it so that D is the probability of fake, while the deck's number-line slides plot the probability of real. The wiki reproduces the formula as printed and states both readings.
Lecture 4's slides 40-41 (disentanglement, beta-VAEs) are not discussed in the talk; the wiki covers them from the slides alone.

Lecture 5's Q-loss (slide 30) is printed as the expectation of a squared norm, and described aloud as an absolute value; asked whether the target, which contains Q(s', a'), depends on the network, the lecturer calls it 'the actual reward' and the notation 'probably a misnomer'. The wiki reports both as the course states them.
Lecture 5 showed, in answer to a question, a slide on training game-playing agents from scratch that is not in the published deck; the wiki describes it from the talk alone.

Lecture 6 states the universal approximation theorem for 'a single layer' (slide 12) and 'a single hidden layer' aloud, and draws it with an unlabelled five-column network; it calls VAE/GAN failure 'Mode collapse' on slide 48 and 'model collapse' aloud. It prints no formula for the diffusion loss or the next-token cross-entropy, and the wiki writes none.

Lecture 7 is a guest lecture (Douglas Blank, Comet ML) built around live demonstrations in Comet's Opik platform. The password-checking metric, the four-model comparison chart (GPT-4o Mini 78%, GPT-4o 94%, GPT-5 100%; no score stated for Gemini 2.5 Flash) and the agent's tool code were shown on screen and are not in the deck; the wiki reports them from the talk alone. The captions garble the first naming of the four models (restored from later in the talk, with an [Ed] note) and break off briefly at about 8:44 and 42:52.

Lecture 7's deck carries no licence notice of its own; it is hosted on the course site, which states that all its materials are under the MIT licence, and LICENSE.md credits it to Douglas Blank as well as to the course.
